sentences.text: Can I hear you now?
Go ahead.

How you doing?
How's things?
Sorry, my, my audio wasn't working there.
How are you?
Yeah I'm good, thank you.
How you doing?
Whereabouts?
Not too bad, Manchester.
Ah, got strong Manchester accent there.
No, I'm Irish but I live in Manchester.
Nice.
Whereabouts in Manchester are you?
So Alford just beside Dean's git.
Yeah.
Okay, cool.
All right.

Oh, small world, Small world.
Whereabouts he from?
Where is she from?
Donegal and Kingsland and a bit of Dublin as well.
Okay, very nice, very nice.
And I'm from St.
Anne's.
Do you know Lilham?
St.
Anne's on the coast near Blackpool.
Sit ons.

I don't see any.
I've never been.
Same direction.
Yeah, don't worry about it.
Good to get a call in with you.
Sorry I got phone calls going off left, right and center as I just put do not disturb on.
No worries.
Yeah, good, good to get a call in with you.
So these calls are really about just learning about your company and what it is that you're trying to achieve and then obviously we can go through some ways that we can help you if that's possible.
So a little bit of background about us.
I don't know how much you know about Capital A, but Capital A is an M and A advisory for marketing services companies.
So we work with marketing agencies or buyers of marketing agencies, both buying the sell side and we own the platform agencies co, which is our marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell.
And on the side we work with private equity or private investors as well as high growth agencies that are looking to make acquisitions as well.
So we get to see both the buy and the sell side which is good for us and good for our clients.
So it'd be great to learn a little bit about you Dylan and what it is that you're doing.
I know you run Maverick Socials on a few different levels, don't you?
So yeah, so I have Maverick Socials which is just kind of like a full scale digital marketing agency, mostly Facebook ads.

And I have then agency Accelerator which is a coaching company that helps marketing agencies, mostly beginners or maybe someone who has maybe five to ten clients scale up to you know, a multi six figure run rate.
And then my holding company is Veneer Investments where I had planned on doing a roll up or what I do plan on doing a roll Up.
I tried to do my first acquisition maybe about 18 months ago and basically the deal got right up to legals with a.

The deed structure was 200k on day one and then 300k deferred over three years and we raised about 200k which is incredibly difficult to do through convention and conventional banks and got to legals and basically the buyer pulled out or not the buyer, the seller pulled out right at the very end and I kind of absorbed the fees and stuff like that.
So yeah, I was badly advised on that one and the guy.
I wasn't doing a program or anything like that.
I kind of had a one on one M&A consultant working with me in that and I was poorly advised.
So since then I've just kind of focused on my businesses that I have now and yeah, I guess looking for the right opportunity to go back in because ultimately long term I do want to do a roll up.
So just I've played around with a few different programs and things like that but up until this point, right now I've just been focusing on growing my actual day to day businesses.
And what was the poor advice that you got from the M and A guy?
Well, first and foremost he didn't want me to go after marketing agencies because they were hard to finance.
He was saying that private equity didn't have a big appetite for them because a lot of them were owner operated, a lot of them were clunky, their clients weren't blue chip.
Like he was kind of putting me off the idea to, to go after marketing agencies.
But in, in a way he wasn't wrong.
Like a lot, there are a lot of agencies like that and to find the good ones it can be difficult.

So we were kind of branching off into different sectors and it ended up being a mistake because even if that deal did go through, I wouldn't have felt totally comfortable going in and applying my skills and knowledge and expertise to it because it wasn't actually in the, the marketing sector.
So you give me bad advice on that.
Like going back I would have just stuck to the same sector.
And yeah, he was, he wanted me to heavily leverage assets on the finance which left quite a lot of cash flow issues, especially with depreciation.
So, and there was just bits and pieces to summarize.
I would just stay in the marketing sector and apply my strengths to any acquisition going forward.
All right, okay.
I would say generally speaking he's not giving you bad advice.
There's um.
What was your way of financing a deal if you were to go into a, a marketing agency and, and acquire it.
What was the, what was the finance that you had in place for that?
Would that have just been self funded?
So do you mean like if I was to do a deal now or are you talking about the deal that we did previously?
Well, both then and now.
How would you finance the acquisition?
If I was to finance an acquisition now, obviously it would massively depend on the, the deal itself.
I have friends, like there's a guy, I wouldn't say he's a friend, he's a guy I know.
He's kind of grown an SEO group and he doesn't put any money into them.
He just uses a mixture of the, the cash and bank with seller finance.
Maybe raises a little bit here and there but very, very rarely puts his money in.
I have another guy, I know it does bigger deals and he just uses a mix of bank finance and seller finance.
If I was to do a deal going forward, I would just pay someone who knows what they're doing to tell me what to do because I've never done it, so I don't know the best way to do it.
So.
Yeah.
Does that answer your question?
Well, yeah, I guess so.
I guess so.

It's just that, you know, you said the M A guy gave you bad advice and just trying to figure out which part of that is bad because if you don't have a huge access to your own capital, then leveraging assets in the target company is definitely the way to go.
And it is tricky with service companies.
It's not just marketing agencies because he's definitely wrong about the private equity side of things.
They have an appetite for marketing agencies for sure.
But the problem is getting the finance in place because you can't get that finance on any assets within a marketing business because they just don't have it.
Sorry, I left out probably a bit of vital information.
So the acquisition was a logistics company in the south of England.
They were doing about a million turnover.
Pretty big company.
They're doing about a million turnover but they were in the south of England.
After the fact, we realized that the owner was, you know, massively inflating how passive the business was.
So I would have been, it was a blessing disguise.
I would have been walking into a business on the other side of the country that I knew nothing about.
And, and it was heavily leveraged on assets that were massively depreciating.
So yeah, got a bit of deal heat with it and it was just dragging on and dragging on and dragging on.
But yeah, that was.
He he was like, you know, go logistics company finance, the trucks, you know, removal company finance, the vehicles.
Like we're all over the place trying to just, you know, the asset finance was driving the strategy rather than the, you know, actually having a proper strategy to roll up a group of companies.
Seem a bit crazy getting a logistics company, but yeah, fair enough.

I've just heard that strategy before in a similar way where it could work where you're, where you're not, where you're not going into marketing agencies and help them be better marketing agencies, but you go into boring companies and help them market better using your skill set, which is a, it is a good, solid strategy for sure, but, but obviously not one that you're looking to do.
So in terms of the roll up that you want to do, how far have you, you got with, with that strategy?
Or are you kind of a, you know, back to square one with putting things together?
Yeah, back to square one.
As I said it was that kind of experience, I guess put me off for lack of a better term.
And yeah, I just thought I'll park that for now and revisit it when I have a little bit more experience.
I've spoke to a few more people and maybe got a little bit more clarity about what I want to do.
So yeah, I just parked that for the time being.
So can you talk me through maybe a little bit about what, what the plan is around a roll up.
So yeah, because you asked about our roll up services.
So yes, I could talk you through what they are.
Yeah.
So my plan is to acquire 5 to 10 companies, get up to 2 to 3 million EIDA and exit over a 4 to 5 year period.
That's basically the plan in a nutshell.

And I don't know whether to keep it super specific in terms of stay in one vertical like performance marketing agencies or go broad under the umbrella of marketing agencies and go performance ads, SEO, web development.
Not really sure what the best route to go is.
I've spoken to a few people that have private equity connections and they say, you know, the more specific the better.

But I've also spoken to other people that say, you know, if you can almost present a one stop shop in terms of you can cover every single marketing aspect there is and tie it up on a nice bow and have, you know, a lot of blue chip recurring clients, they like that also.
So yeah, you kind of hear different things based on who you speak to.
Yeah, I think they're both solid bits of advice, but obviously they, you can't do the same thing in the same roll up.
But, but certainly if you're looking to, if you, if you're looking to compete in one sort of vertical that's it is definitely a way to go.
What tends to happen is private equity they will buy.
Hello?
Andy, can you hear me?
Andy?
Sorry mate, I think I lost you for a second there.
You just literally cut off.
As you were saying, what tends to happen.

Yeah, so with, with private equity what they're looking for is, is usually a platform business that is doing about 2 million in EBITDA and they want that business to just have a track record of really safe revenue.
So they're not looking to take a gamble.
They're not like VC buyers.
Well investors that are looking to put you know, 100 million into a, a load of bets.

So they a platform business first and then they can bolt all sorts onto it.

You know, broad services.
Yeah but always you're looking for those businesses that have really strong clients with long, long contracts.
So, so yeah, you want, you want big international clients either way.
Yeah, I think maybe.
Have I selected the wrong option?

Okay, yeah.

And then we'd go out, speak to everybody, we'd have those initial conversations, make sure that they're not tire kickers, that they're definitely interested in the idea of selling.
But the important thing is that we're going off market.
We're not looking at load of brokers, we're actually finding agencies that aren't for sale and then trying to bring them in to a deal with you.
I think possibly what you've learned from that last experience was you had one deal, but once that deal fell over, it was difficult then to pick up all the pieces and get going again.

And what we do is we build deal flow.

If you're trying to build a roll up or you're an investor.

Yeah.

So if you were interested in a particular agency, then we'd help you put together, you know, an offer, et cetera, et cetera, to get the deal closed.

Okay.

Are you helping with deal structure?

I mean that's kind of like a traditional deal structure, but the lower end of the market.
I mean it really does depend what size deals you're looking to do.
I mean, do you have an idea of what it is that you're looking put together?

So within reason I would just be go, I would go big from the outset in terms of probably seven figure turnover, maybe 50%.

Okay.
I think in, in.

summary.overview: In an exploratory business discussion meeting, Dylan Power and Andy Day introduced themselves, highlighting their backgrounds and the focus of their respective ventures. Dylan, who operates a digital marketing agency, coaching company, and a holding company, shared insights from a previous M&A attempt that was hindered by poor advice, emphasizing the need for strategic guidance in acquisitions. The conversation progressed to Dylan's roll-up strategy, aiming to acquire 5-10 marketing companies over the next few years to achieve a significant EBITDA for an eventual exit. Andy elaborated on Capital A's role as an M&A advisory for marketing services, detailing their services, pricing structure, and financing strategies, including bank financing and alternative options. The meeting concluded with a focus on aligning business goals and financing considerations for future acquisitions.
summary.short_summary: Dylan Power and Andy Day held a business discussion centered on mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in the marketing services sector. Dylan shared his experience with a previous failed acquisition attempt due to poor advice and emphasized the importance of strategic guidance in M&A. He outlined his roll-up strategy to acquire 5-10 marketing companies over 4-5 years, targeting a significant EBITDA for a future exit. Andy elaborated on Capital A's role as an M&A advisory, detailing their services, pricing structure, and financing strategies, including bank financing and alternative options. The conversation concluded with an emphasis on aligning business goals and the financial considerations necessary for successful acquisitions.
